name: University Building Lofts
award: 2025 Federal 4% and state housing tax credits (Round Two)
headline: Mile High Development and BMC Investments plan to convert the upper 11 floors of the historic 12-story University Building at 910 16th Street in downtown Denver from offices into 120 small apartments for households earning 30% to 80% AMI. The project won 2025 Round Two federal 4%, state and TOC credits from CHFA.
why_it_matters: It is one of Denver's first office-to-affordable conversions financed by the new Downtown Development Authority: a $14.7M TIF-backed loan, approved by Denver City Council in October 2026, sits alongside about $43M of housing and historic tax credit equity in a $73M budget.

status.label: Credits awarded; city funding approved October 2026; closing targeted by March 2027
status.detail: Denver City Council passed the DDDA funding agreement (Council Bill 26-1336) on 2026-10-05, and the Mayor signed it on 2026-10-07. The DDDA loan documents set a closing date on or before 2027-03-31, the same deadline for starting construction, and require a certificate of occupancy by 2028-12-31. A revised concept plan was still under city review in April 2026. No record of an acquisition closing, building permit or construction start was found.

next_step: Watch for the purchase and financing closing (DDDA loan closing by 2027-03-31), the building permit, and the federal historic tax credit Part 2 approval.

key_numbers.value: 120 homes, all income-restricted, in a 1911 landmark
key_numbers.meaning: 57 studios, 52 one-bedroom and 11 two-bedroom units at 30% to 80% AMI, with an average of 59.3% AMI.
About $31M over 10 years, plus $1,800,000 in state credit and $156,000 in TOC credit, with $36,500,000 in CHFA bonds.
The sources and uses in the DDDA loan documents: $8M for the building, $44.6M for construction, and $43.2M of tax credit equity (housing and historic).
A 2% cash-flow loan over 40 years from the Denver Downtown Development Authority, repaid by the project and funded from DDDA tax increment.

facts.value: 910 16th Street (900-918 16th Street), Denver 80202, at 16th and Champa on the former 16th Street Mall
I/F, A/R: individuals/families, acquisition/rehab (adaptive reuse of a commercial building)
Twelve-story concrete office building, about 110,000 sq ft, designed by Fisher & Fisher, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978

A condominium regime: the housing entity buys floors 2 to 12 plus the lobby and part of the basement, and the seller keeps the ground-floor retail (tenants such as Sportsfan and Modern Market are expected to stay)
910 Associates, Inc., which took title from Naiman Family Ltd. Liability Co. LLC by a May 2023 deed recorded as a merger of title
University Building Lofts Owner LLC, a Delaware LLC care of Mile High Development

D-TD, UO-1; multifamily allowed. The city released the project from concept review straight to building permit, skipping the site development plan. A revised concept plan was filed under Denver's Prop 123 fast-track review in April 2026

Full interior renovation of floors 2 to 12: new mechanical, electrical, plumbing and life-safety systems, a new pressurized stair core, repaired or replaced windows and rehabilitated elevators, with no exterior changes. Steam heat is replaced by a four-pipe fan coil system with a central boiler sized for later heat-pump conversion
Community room, fitness center, on-site management, bike storage, public restrooms and space for a food pantry; in-unit washers and dryers where feasible
D, H and L light rail lines 0.1 mile away, free MallRide and MetroRide, Walk Score 98 and Transit Score 87. Residents get RTD NECO passes
Enterprise Green Communities; electrification-ready and solar-ready
In a Small Area Difficult Development Area (basis boost); the applicant asked CHFA to waive its basis limit because of historic adaptive reuse costs

money.note: Awarded in 2025 Round Two. Amounts are as CHFA's award report prints them.

money.source: Colorado accelerated state housing tax credit

money.note: CHFA is issuer. The application planned a private placement with KeyBank, with $23,000,000 retired at completion, plus about $12,000,000 of taxable construction debt. The DDDA documents cap senior debt at $45M before and $18M after permanent loan closing; the budget shows a $13,360,000 permanent loan.

2% interest compounding annually, paid from excess cash flow and refinancing proceeds, 40-year maturity, nonrecourse and subordinate to senior debt. It may not pay for the building purchase. The money is advanced by the City from the DDDA's PNC loan, repaid from DDDA tax increment. The DDDA board approved the loan on 2026-06-24 and the funding agreement on 2026-08-26; Council passed CB 26-1336 on 2026-10-05.

money.source: Federal and state housing and historic tax credit equity
money.note: The DDDA loan documents name PNC Bank as federal limited partner and a Sugar Creek Capital affiliate as state limited partner.
Developer and consultant fees total $7,416,079 in the budget.
In return the seller gets a 20% non-controlling stake in the project's manager entity, with no say and no developer fee, per the applicant.

background.text: Mile High Development first applied for the project in CHFA's 2024 Round Two with the same 120-unit mix and a Warren Village services partnership. It was not among the 2024 Round Two awards.

For the 2025 application the team cut the purchase price from $13M to $8M, added Heritage Consulting for historic credits, dropped Warren Village because of capacity limits, added TOC credits and secured a preliminary DDDA award of up to $15M.

The DDDA board approved the owner's petition to bring the property into the DDDA on 2025-07-30 and announced $14.5M for the project that day in its first $100M funding round. Council approved the inclusion by ordinance (file 26-1187), passed in September 2026.

The DDDA project summary in the funding agreement says construction would begin by December 2025, while the loan agreement attached to it sets a 2027-03-31 deadline to start construction and 2028-12-31 for a certificate of occupancy.
The DDDA loan requires CHFA tax credit financing for all 120 affordable units and the purchase to close before any loan money is paid out, and the borrower must follow all CHFA covenant terms.
The applicant says the building is occupied, earlier owners spent little on capital work while expecting a sale, and no public money has gone into the building before.
A 2023 City of Denver and Gensler study scored the building 91%, the highest of the downtown buildings it checked for office-to-residential conversion.

The market study shows a 14.1% overall capture rate, with high capture at 40% to 60% AMI and a thin gap between maximum tax credit rents and market rents. The applicant sets its 70% and 80% AMI rents below the maximum.
There are no homeless set-aside units or project-based vouchers in the application. The downtown neighborhood organization and Mayor Mike Johnston sent letters of support.

discrepancies.text: The DDDA loan is $14,700,000 in the funding agreement and council bill request, while Colorado Politics and Naked Denver reported $14.5 million in July and August 2025 and the application cited a preliminary award of up to $15,000,000.
The application says KeyBank CDC proposed to buy the federal and state credits, while the DDDA loan documents name PNC Bank as federal investor and a Sugar Creek Capital affiliate as state investor.
The 2025 application and Naked Denver say the building was built in 1911, while the 2024 application says 1910.
The application puts the permanent bonds at what reads as $13.5 million ($36.5M less $23M retired), while the DDDA budget shows a $13,360,000 permanent loan.
